messages.subject: custom skewed t distribution
parts:
Dear colleagues!

I am trying to implement custom distribution for fitting parameters of data from my experiments. But my model works extremely slow and returns incorrect results (mu = 29 vs mu = 718 etc).

I attached the description of this distribution, also you can find it here, p.189, part A.3.14.
Usually I work with this distribution using gamlss R-package (this distribution denoted in gamlss package as ST5).


I would be happy if you could tell me what is wrong with my model:

model <- "
        data {
            int <lower=1> N;
            vector [N] y;
        }
        parameters {
            real mu;
            real<lower=0> sigma;
            real nu;
            real<lower=0> tau;
            vector<lower=0,upper=1> [N] bc;
        }
        transformed parameters {
            real<lower=0> a;
            real<lower=0> b;
            vector<lower=0> [N] c;
            vector [N] z;
            vector [N] sq;
            a <- (2/tau + 2 * nu/(tau * sqrt(2 * tau + nu * nu)))/2;
            b <- (2/tau - 2 * nu/(tau * sqrt(2 * tau + nu * nu)))/2;
            for (n in 1:N) {
              c[n] <- 1/(pow(2, a + b - 1) * sqrt(a + b) * bc[n]);
              z[n] <- (y[n] - mu)/sigma;
              sq[n] <-  z[n]/sqrt(a + b + z[n] * z[n]);
            }

        }
        model {
            bc ~ beta(a, b);
            increment_log_prob(log(c/sigma) + (a + 0.5) * log(1 + sq) + (b + 0.5) * log(1 - sq));
        }"

y <- rST5(1000, mu = 718, sigma = 156, nu = 0.6, tau = 0.92)

mcmc_samples <- stan(model_code = model,
                     data = list(N = length(y), y = y),
                     pars = c("mu", "sigma", "nu", "tau", "a", "b"),
                     chains = 1, iter = 300, warmup = 100, verbose = F)

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: custom skewed t distribution
parts:
On Sunday, July 19, 2015 at 1:35:10 PM UTC-4, Philipp Upravitelev wrote:
bc in my model replaces B(a, b) in the definition of the c parameter

look:
c = [(2^(a+b-1)) * ((a+b)^0.5) * B(a, b)]^(-1)

But that is not a separate parameter to be declared in the parameters block but rather a conditionally deterministic function of a and b (which are in turn conditionally deterministic functions of tau and nu. This st5.stan file is logically correct

functions {
  real st5_log(vector x, real mu, real sigma, real nu, real tau) {
    int N;
    vector[rows(x)] z;
    real ve;
    real lam;
    real a;
    real b;
    real aphalf;
    real bphalf;
    vector[rows(x)] kernel;
    if (sigma <= 0) reject("sigma must be positive");
    if (tau <= 0) reject("tau must be positive");
    z <- (x - mu) / sigma;
    ve <- 2 / tau;
    lam <- 2 * nu / (tau * sqrt(2 * tau + square(nu)));
    a <- (ve + lam) / 2;
    b <- (ve - lam) / 2;
    aphalf <- a + 0.5;
    bphalf <- b + 0.5;
    N <- rows(x);
    for (i in 1:N) {
      real fraction;
      fraction <- z[i] / sqrt(ve + square(z[i]));
      kernel[i] <- aphalf * log1p(fraction) + bphalf * log1m(fraction);
    }
    return sum(kernel) - N * ( (ve - 1) * log(2) + 0.5 * log(ve) +
                               lbeta(a, b) + log(sigma) );

}
}
data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  vector[N] y;
}
parameters {
  real mu;
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  real nu;
  real<lower=0> tau;
}

model {
  y ~ st5(mu, sigma, nu, tau);
}

where by "logically correct", I mean if you do (with rstan 2.7.0)

library(rstan)
library(gamlss)
y <- rST5(1000, mu = 718, sigma = 156, nu = 0.6, tau = 0.92)

expose_stan_functions("st5.stan") # puts st5_log in .GlobalEnv
all.equal(sum(dST5(y, mu = 718, sigma = 156, nu = 0.6, tau = 0.92, log = TRUE)),
          st5_log(y, mu = 718, sigma = 156, nu = 0.6, tau = 0.92))

However, with those parameter values you are going to need a good bit of prior information to recover them.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: custom skewed t distribution
parts:
On Monday, July 20, 2015 at 9:02:36 AM UTC-4, Philipp Upravitelev wrote:
Could you give me advice what distributions I should declare as the distributions of the priors? 
In my opinion I should use lognormal distribution. Am I right?

It's pretty tough to say what is right. Saying what is wrong is easier and lognormal would be wrong for mu and nu because they are defined over the entire real line. A lognormal might be okay for sigma and tau but there are lots of other distributions for positive random variables. Basically use whatever prior distribution you want.

Ben
